The growth trajectory of Angolan dentex (Dentex angolensis) has been characterized through field sampling and otolith-based back-calculation, allowing for robust estimates of size at key life stages. Upon hatching, the free-swimming larva emerges from a pelagic egg with a remarkably small body mass. From egg diameter data for related sparids, the wet weight at birth has been estimated at approximately 0.00032 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00032 grams], reflecting the modest energetic reserves contained within the yolk sac. This initial mass, typical of small pelagic teleost larvae, supports a brief endotrophic phase before first exogenous feeding must commence. The transition occurs rapidly, and the subsequent allometric growth during the planktonic larval period is substantial. Body size increases considerably as the larva develops through the preflexion and postflexion stages, culminating in the larval-juvenile transition. The ultimate total length achieved by adults in natural populations has been recorded as 37.5 centimeters [Li = 37.5 centimeters], a value that positions the species among the medium-bodied members of the family Sparidae and represents the asymptotic size typical of fully grown individuals in the region.

Reproductive development in this species is closely linked to the attainment of a specific body length, which serves as a reliable proxy for the onset of gonadal maturation. Field surveys have consistently indicated that puberty is initiated once individuals reach a total length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters]. This size threshold marks the beginning of gametogenesis and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, although active spawning may not commence immediately. At this pivotal length, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been calculated using length-weight relationships derived from local stock assessments, yielding a value of approximately 54 grams [Wwp = approximately 54 grams]. This body mass represents a substantial increase from the larval stage, reflecting the accumulation of somatic tissues necessary to support the energetic demands of future reproductive events. The relationship between length and mass remains consistent throughout the juvenile and sub-adult phases, governed by the isometric or slightly allometric scaling typical of sparid fishes along the West African continental shelf.

At a stable water temperature of 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C], the gonadosomatic index (GSI) for mature individuals was measured at 5% [GSI = 5%] and the age at birth has been documented as 4 days [ab = 4 days]. The age at birth, defined as the duration from egg fertilization to larval eclosion, reflects the accelerated developmental rate afforded by relatively warm subtropical waters and facilitates rapid progression through the vulnerable yolk-sac phase. Comparative studies with congeneric species, particularly Dentex dentex, have provided valuable insights into the reproductive physiology and longevity of Angolan dentex when evaluated under controlled thermal conditions.

Long-term mark-recapture programs and otolith age readings have furnished reliable estimates of the total lifespan of Dentex angolensis in its natural habitat. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of the eastern Atlantic, which average around 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C], the species exhibits a maximum documented longevity of 17 years [am = 17 years]. This considerable lifespan is comparable to that of other long-lived sparids, including Dentex dentex, and reflects a life history strategy that balances relatively slow somatic growth with extended reproductive tenure. Coinciding with the accumulation of biomass over this long lifetime, the ultimate wet weight reached by the largest, oldest individuals in the population has been estimated at 870 grams [Wwi = 870 grams]. This asymptotic mass, derived from the length-weight conversion formula specific to the stock, underscores the species capacity to achieve a substantial body size over the course of its multi-decadal existence, with implications for both fecundity and trophic position within the benthic community.

The interplay between size at maturity and the overall growth trajectory governs the reproductive output and population dynamics of Angolan dentex. Individuals that attain the pubertal length of 15 centimeters [Lp = 15 centimeters] and its corresponding mass of approximately 54 grams [Wwp = approximately 54 grams] do so relatively early in their extended lifespan, leaving a prolonged window for iteroparous spawning events. The high ultimate body mass of 870 grams [Wwi = 870 grams] that characterizes the oldest adults is a product of continued somatic investment over 17 years [am = 17 years], a timeframe that allows for multiple reproductive seasons at a temperature of 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C]. The gonadosomatic index of 5% [GSI = 5%] was measured at 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C]. This reproductive strategy, combined with the brief 4-day incubation period (4 days) [ab = 4 days] at the same temperature, suggests an adaptation to relatively stable subtropical conditions where moderate, sustained investment in reproduction is favored over a single, high-intensity spawning event.
